newsitem.title: GERMANY: Russia wants high price for bigger NATO - Kinkel.
newsitem.headline: Russia wants high price for bigger NATO - Kinkel.

text.p: German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said on Tuesday Russia demanded a high price for accepting NATO expansion and the alliance must discuss many military, economic and diplomatic issues to make it palatable to Moscow.
Russia knew it could not stop the alliance from expanding into ex-communist eastern Europe but would need a wide range of reassurances that the move was not aimed against it, he said.

Kinkel, who said he had been briefed on Chancellor Helmut Kohl's talks on Saturday with Russian President Boris Yeltsin, also characterised Moscow's renewed tough line against a larger NATO as "a strategy, not a counter-strategy."
"The Russians are trying to make the price for NATO expansion as favourable to themselves as possible," he told journalists in Bonn. "But Russia knows it cannot block NATO expansion."

Kinkel said talks on NATO expansion would also cover the Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) treaty, the START-2 nuclear arms reduction treaty, Moscow's role in the Group of Seven industrialised states and economic aid for Russia.

NATO and Russia should also consider creating a permanent consultation body he has proposed with equal rights for Russia to discuss disarmament, non-proliferation of mass destruction weapons, peacekeeping and other global issues, Kinkel said.
NATO could also use confidence-building measures like its cooperation with Russia in the SFOR peacekeeping forces in Bosnia to convince Moscow of its good intentions, he added.
Kinkel contradicted the sceptical reaction heard in western capitals to the confidence Kohl expressed about a solution to the issue after his talks with Yeltsin.
"The Russians say and will continue to say they're against (NATO expansion)," Kinkel said.
"So we'll have to do everything we can with the Russians to convince them they will not be isolated. I'm hopeful, yes I'm convinced we will succeed in the end."

He also saw no hardening of Moscow's line, despite the announcement on Monday that Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov had been asked to prepare a plan of action to respond to steps to welcome former Warsaw Pact members into NATO.
"Nothing has changed since my talks with Primakov," he said, referring to their meeting last September.
NATO countries already agreed at last month's Lisbon summit on European security to adapt the 1990 CFE arms reduction pact to post-Cold War realities.
Russia has pushed for a change since the Soviet Union broke up in 1991 and western officials fear Moscow might demand a higher arms quota because of the NATO expansion plan.

Opposition from the Russian military has so far held up Moscow's ratification of the START-2 treaty with the United States, which would slash long-range nuclear warheads to one-third of their Cold War levels.

The rich man's club called the G7 -- made up of the United States, Japan, Germany, Britain, France, Italy and Canada -- has made Russia a partner to its political discussions but kept Moscow out of its annual talks on finetuning the world economy.
Kinkel said his proposed "S-17" body, a permanent security body made up of the 16 NATO states and Russia, could deal with issues like how consultation mechanisms would work.

The minister suggested the idea last month, saying it would allow NATO to divide its decisions into those it could take unilaterally, those it consulted with Moscow on and those on which it needed consensus with Russia before taking.
Kinkel said NATO would probably accept a small group of new members in a first wave and would face problems reassuring those left out that the alliance door was not shut completely.
He did not say which countries would be invited in a first wave but said the lists of first new members in NATO and the European Union would probably be the same.
He said Estonia presented a special problem as it would probably qualify for the EU earlier than the other two Baltic states. "Can we pull Estonia out of this trio?" he asked.

Kinkel added: "If country A is not in the first group, it could get an expanded Partnership for Peace programme and other bilateral and multilateral aid to help it get over this period when people think they have been left behind."
